questions.question: Why does every form control need a label?
options: It makes the form accessible to vision-impaired users.
questions.explanation: each form control should have its own label as this makes the form accessible to vision-impaired users.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: each form control should have its own <label> element as this makes the form accessible to vision-impaired users.

questions.question: Which pattern labels an input by wrapping?
questions.explanation: label can wrap the description and the form input.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: Wrap around both the text description and the form input

questions.question: Inclusive Components' first widget chapter is about?
questions.explanation: The inaugural chapter explores what it takes to make toggle buttons inclusive.

reference.excerpt: In this inaugural chapter, I’ll be exploring what it takes to make toggle buttons inclusive.

questions.question: Are toggle buttons all alike?
options: Yes; one markup fits every product.
No. Purpose is simple, but applications and forms vary, and it is easy to forget a requirement.
questions.explanation: on/off switches are not all alike. Plenty to forget to do.

reference.excerpt: yet on/off switches (or toggle buttons) are not all alike.

questions.question: What misconception does Pickering call out about screen readers?
options: That they understand every ARIA attribute automatically.
That they require tables for layout.
questions.explanation: A popular misconception has been that screen readers don't understand JavaScript. That is untrue.

reference.excerpt: A popular misconception has been that screen readers don’t understand JavaScript.

questions.question: What are the primitives of interactive forms?
questions.explanation: Form elements are the primitives of interactive UIs. Native controls already have names and keyboard behavior.

reference.excerpt: Form elements are the primitives of interactiv

questions.question: Why is delete-on-hover a problem?
options: Screen readers only work with hover.
questions.explanation: The delete functionality only appears on hover, making it an entirely inaccessible feature by keyboard.

reference.excerpt: the delete functionality only appears on hover, making it an entirely inaccessible feature by keyboard.

questions.question: Which button is named for assistive tech?
questions.explanation: Visible text is the accessible name. An empty button has no name. A nameless div is worse.

reference.excerpt: what it takes to make toggle buttons inclusive

questions.question: Which image alt is correct for a meaningful photo?
questions.explanation: alt should give an accurate description of the image content so it can be understood by screen reader software.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: It should give an accurate description of the image content so it can be understood by screen reader software

questions.question: A decorative divider still needs which alt?
options: Omit alt so screen readers skip the tag.
alt="" — the attribute is there, the value is empty.
questions.explanation: If the image is only decoration, alt should still be used but the quotes should be left empty.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
reference.excerpt: then the alt attribute should still be used but the quotes should be left

questions.question: Which toggle exposes pressed state?
questions.explanation: aria-pressed is the state Inclusive Components styles for on/off buttons. There is no <toggle> tag.

questions.question: Do basic state changes always require JavaScript?
options: No. Native controls communicate state without a custom script.
questions.explanation: Basic state changes, communicated both visually and to assistive technology, do not necessarily depend on JavaScript.

reference.excerpt: basic state changes, communicated both visually and to assistive technology software, do not necessarily depend on JavaScript to take place anyway.

questions.question: Which delete control can a keyboard user reach?
options: A trash icon that exists only in :hover CSS.
A real <button>Delete</button> that stays in the DOM.
questions.explanation: If it only appears on hover, it is not a keyboard feature. Keep a button in the document.

reference.excerpt: making it an entirely inaccessible feature by keyboard

questions.question: What should you do instead of a custom div checkbox?
options: Keep the div and add tabindex="0" only.
Paint a check with CSS and skip HTML.
questions.explanation: Form elements are the primitives. A native checkbox already has a name, a value, and keyboard behavior.

reference.excerpt: Form elements are the primitives of interactiv

questions.question: Which pairing is accessible?
options: <input id="age" type="text" name="age"><label>Age</label> with no for.
questions.explanation: for matches id. Placeholder is not a label. A nearby word with no for is not wired.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett
